document.title: The Wreck of the Titan: Or, Futility
document.author: Morgan Robertson

quotes.quote: She was the largest craft afloat and the greatest of the works of men.
the steamship _Titan_ was considered practically unsinkable.

Unsinkable--indestructible, she carried as few boats as would satisfy the laws. These, twenty-four in number, were securely covered and lashed down to their chocks on the upper deck, and if launched would hold five hundred people.
for, though it was April, the salt air was chilly
"Ice," yelled the lookout; "ice ahead. Iceberg. Right under the bows."
Seventy-five thousand tons--dead-weight--rushing through the fog at the rate of fifty feet a second, had hurled itself at an iceberg.

differs: The text read here, Project Gutenberg's, is the 1912 Autograph Edition, which carries both "Copyright, 1898, by M. F. MANSFIELD" and "Copyright, 1912, by MORGAN ROBERTSON"; the tellers speak of the 1898 book, and the wording of the 1898 first edition is not checked here and may differ from the 1912 text quoted.

passages.text: My first observations positively terrified me, as there was present in them something mysterious, not to say supernatural, and I was alone in my laboratory at night; but at that time the idea of these disturbances being intelligently controlled signals did not yet present itself to me.
The changes I noted were taking place periodically, and with such a clear suggestion of number and order that they were not traceable to any cause then known to me.

The feeling is constantly growing on me that I had been the first to hear the greeting of one planet to another. A purpose was behind these electrical signals; and it was with this conviction that I announced to the Red Cross Society, when it asked me to indicate one of the great possible achievements of the next hundred years, that it would probably be the confirmation and interpretation of this planetary challenge to us.

differs: In Talking with Planets, an article in Collier's Weekly in 1901, Tesla writes that at his Colorado laboratory he recorded electrical changes with "a clear suggestion of number and order" that he came to feel were "the greeting of one planet to another"; he describes hearing signals, not speaking or communicating with anyone, and writes of an answer as something still to come.

document.title: AMC Opinion Concerning "Flying Discs" (the Twining memo)
document.author: Nathan Twining
document.issuer: Air Materiel Command, US Army Air Forces

passages.text: The phenomenon reported is something real and not visionary or fictitious.

The reported operating characteristics such as extreme rates of climb, maneuverability (particularly in roll), and action which must be considered evasive when sighted or contacted by friendly aircraft and radar, lend belief to the possibility that some of the objects are controlled either manually, automatically or remotely.

It is possible within the present U. S. knowledge -- provided extensive detailed development is undertaken -- to construct a piloted aircraft which has the general description of the object in sub-paragraph (e) above which would be capable of an approximate range of 7000 miles at subsonic speeds.

Any developments in this country along the lines indicated would be extremely expensive, time consuming and at the considerable expense of current projects and therefore, if directed, should be set up independently of existing projects.
The possibility that these objects are of domestic origin - the product of some high security project not known to AC/AS-2 or this Command.

differs: The letter's own words (paragraph 2a) are "something real and not visionary or fictitious", where some tellers say "neither visionary nor fictitious". What the host calls the memo's postscript is in the body of the letter: paragraph 2f says a piloted aircraft of the objects' description could be built within present US knowledge, and paragraph 2g that any such development, if directed, "should be set up independently of existing projects"; the letter does not mention the Manhattan Project.

document.title: The Book of Enoch (translated by R. H. Charles)

passages.text: And it came to pass when the children of men had multiplied that in those days were born unto them beautiful and comely daughters.
And the angels, the children of the heaven, saw and lusted after them, and said to one another: ‘Come, let us choose us wives from among the children of men and beget us children.’

And they were in all two hundred; who descended ⌈in the days⌉ of Jared on the summit of Mount Hermon, and they called it Mount Hermon, because they had sworn and bound themselves by mutual imprecations upon it.

And all the others together with them took unto themselves wives, and each chose for himself one, and they began to go in unto them and to defile themselves with them, and they taught them charms and enchantments, and the cutting of roots, and made them acquainted with plants.
And they became pregnant, and they bare great giants, whose height was three thousand ells:

Есть факты, которым мы не верим, пока они не коснутся нас самих.

differs: Tsiolkovsky's 1928 pamphlet Unknown Intelligent Forces, in the Russian Wikisource text read here (which may not be the whole pamphlet), says an influence on us of living beings "like us, only more perfect" is very possible, and that some facts speak for the intervention of incomprehensible forces in human acts; the word angel does not appear in it, and it tells of no contact of his own.

document.title: Ether and the Theory of Relativity
document.author: Albert Einstein

quotes.quote: Recapitulating, we may say that according to the general theory of relativity space is endowed with physical qualities; in this sense, therefore, there exists an ether.
quotes.locator: Ether and the Theory of Relativity

quotes.quote: According to the general theory of relativity space without ether is unthinkable; for in such space there not only would be no propagation of light, but also no possibility of existence for standards of space and time (measuring-rods and clocks), nor therefore any space-time intervals in the physical sense.
quotes.locator: Ether and the Theory of Relativity

quotes.quote: But this ether may not be thought of as endowed with the quality characteristic of ponderable media, as consisting of parts which may be tracked through time. The idea of motion may not be applied to it.
quotes.locator: Ether and the Theory of Relativity

quotes.quote: More careful reflection teaches us, however, that the special theory of relativity does not compel us to deny ether.
quotes.locator: Ether and the Theory of Relativity

differs: Ether and the Theory of Relativity is an address, not a paper: the text in Einstein's Sidelights on Relativity reads "An Address delivered on May 5th, 1920, in the University of Leyden", so neither the host's 1923 nor Salvatore Pais's 1921 matches its date.
